title: The k-th Smallest Number in a Range

concept.title: Keep one version of a counting tree for every prefix, and subtract two versions to see exactly the range
body: A list is fixed and every question asks for the **k-th smallest number among the positions `l..r`**. For `5 2 9 2 7` and the range 2 to 4 the numbers are `2 9 2`, and the 2nd smallest is 2. Sorting every range costs O(n log n) per question, and the answers cannot be combined from simpler pieces because order statistics are not additive.

Compress the values to ranks `0..m-1`. A **counting tree** over the ranks tells, for any set of numbers, how many of them fall in a rank interval, and it can find the k-th element by descending: go left if the left half holds at least `k` numbers, otherwise subtract that count and go right. Now build a **persistent** version: version `i` is the counting tree of the first `i` numbers. Inserting the next number creates only the O(log m) nodes on one path and shares everything else with the previous version, so all versions together take O(n log m) nodes.

body.code:
for x in a:                                   # version i + 1 from version i
    new root; copy the path to rank[x] with count + 1; children not on the path are shared

def kth(l, r, k):                             # versions l - 1 and r
    u, w = roots[l - 1], roots[r]
    while lo < hi:
        c = ct[left[w]] - ct[left[u]]         # numbers of the range in the left half
        if k <= c: u, w, hi = left[u], left[w], mid
        else:      k -= c; u, w, lo = right[u], right[w], mid + 1

body: The difference of the counts of two versions is exactly the count over the range, so the descent runs on the two trees in parallel. A question costs O(log m). The answer is the value that belongs to the final rank. Equal numbers have equal ranks and are counted with their multiplicity.

statement: A list of `n` numbers is given. Answer `q` questions. Each question has three numbers `l`, `r` and `k`: among the numbers at the positions `l` to `r` (counting from 1, both included), find the `k`-th smallest one. Equal numbers are counted separately: in `2 2 5` the 2nd smallest is 2. Print the answers on one line, in the order of the questions.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `q`: the length of the list and the number of questions.
The second line has the `n` numbers of the list.
Each of the next `q` lines has three numbers `l`, `r` and `k`.

examples.note: The whole list sorted is 2 2 5 7 9, whose 3rd is 5. The range 2..4 holds 2 9 2, whose 2nd smallest is 2. The range 3..5 holds 9 2 7, whose smallest is 2: 5 2 2.

hints: Compress the values and think of a segment tree over the ranks that counts how many numbers fall in each interval of ranks.
Build a persistent version of that tree after every prefix of the list, sharing all the nodes that did not change.
The counts of the versions r and l - 1 differ by exactly the range; descend in both trees at once to find the k-th.

explanation: A persistent counting tree over the ranks of the values has one version per prefix of the list. The counts of the versions r and l - 1 differ by exactly the range, and a parallel descent finds the k-th smallest.
solution.complexity: Time O((n + q) log n), space O(n log n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, q = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
qs = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

vals = sorted(set(a))
rank = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
m = len(vals)
lc = [0]
rc = [0]
ct = [0]
roots = [0]
for x in a:
    v = rank[x]
    prev = roots[-1]
    cur = len(ct)
    roots.append(cur)
    lc.append(0)
    rc.append(0)
    ct.append(ct[prev] + 1)
    lo = 0
    hi = m - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        nn = len(ct)
        lc.append(0)
        rc.append(0)
        if v <= mid:
            rc[cur] = rc[prev]
            lc[cur] = nn
            ct.append(ct[lc[prev]] + 1)
            prev = lc[prev]
            hi = mid
        else:
            lc[cur] = lc[prev]
            rc[cur] = nn
            ct.append(ct[rc[prev]] + 1)
            prev = rc[prev]
            lo = mid + 1
        cur = nn
out = []
for l, rr, k in qs:
    u = roots[l - 1]
    w = roots[rr]
    lo = 0
    hi = m - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        c = ct[lc[w]] - ct[lc[u]]
        if k <= c:
            u = lc[u]
            w = lc[w]
            hi = mid
        else:
            k -= c
            u = rc[u]
            w = rc[w]
            lo = mid + 1
    out.append(vals[lo])
print(*out)
